Sup A: bolton_2006_cake_intermediate_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Cake-intermediate blocking)
The cake-intermediate blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous or virus-retention membranes. It predicts permeate volume over time during constant-pressure operation and pressure rise over time during constant-flow operation. The model combines loss of available membrane area through intermediate blocking with increasing flow resistance from cake formation, using Darcy’s law to derive explicit time-dependent equations. The authors evaluated it with human plasma IgG filtered through Durapore PVDF membranes and BSA filtered through Viresolve 180 membranes, under both constant-pressure and constant-flow conditions. They fitted two parameters by minimizing squared residuals and compared its predictions with individual and other combined fouling models.

Sup B: bolton_2006_complete_standard_blocking · Combined models of membrane fouling: Development and application to microfiltration and ultrafiltration of biological fluids (Complete-standard blocking)
The Complete-standard blocking model describes fouling during filtration of biological fluids through microporous membranes by combining complete pore blockage with standard blocking, in which deposits constrict pores. It predicts permeate volume over time at constant pressure and pressure over time at constant flow, using explicit relationships derived from Darcy’s law. The model has two fitted fouling parameters and is intended for cases where both mechanisms are relevant; it reduces to the corresponding single-mechanism model when one mechanism dominates. The paper compares its fits with individual fouling models using sterile filtration data for human plasma IgG and virus-filtration data for BSA, collected in small membrane holders. Across the reported comparisons, the combined model fit about as well as standard blocking alone, while other combined models performed better for some data sets. The authors present the combined models as tools for fitting fouling curves and assessing membrane sizing, while noting that a good fit does not establish the physical mechanism.
